title: New Arrivals Reshape Vanuatu
text: Ancient DNA from Efate and Epi shows that people of almost entirely Papuan ancestry had reached Vanuatu by around 2,300 years ago, coming from the Bismarck Archipelago rather than the closer Solomon Islands. Yet the islanders kept speaking the Austronesian language of the first Lapita settlers, and its descendants, more than 120 languages, are still spoken in Vanuatu today.

source.name: Current Biology (Lipson et al. 2018, via PubMed Central): Population Turnover in Remote Oceania Shortly after Initial Settlement

source2.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History: Ancient DNA reveals genetic replacement despite language continuity in the South Pacific

title: Settlers on Tiny Fais Island
place: Fais Island, Yap State, Federated States of Micronesia
text: Fais is a raised coral island of just 2.8 square kilometres, with no safe anchorage, about 80 km from Ulithi atoll. Its earliest layer, radiocarbon-dated to about AD 230–410, held giant-clam shell adzes, shell bracelets and beads, and a few potsherds. Rats arrived with the first settlers, and pots kept coming over the sea from Yap throughout the island's history.

source.name: Asian Perspectives 47(1), University of Hawai'i ScholarSpace (Intoh 2008): Ongoing Archaeological Research on Fais Island, Micronesia

title: Taro Clues in Swamp Mud
place: Emaotfer Swamp, near Teouma, Efate, Vanuatu
text: A sediment core from Emaotfer swamp, 1 km from the Teouma Lapita cemetery, holds chemical traces of the first settlers. Molecules made by human gut microbes rise at the same time as a marker of taro farming, showing gardens arrived with the newcomers. The first unmistakable sign dates to about 2,800 years ago, during a spell of increasingly wet weather.

source.name: Communications Earth & Environment (2024, via PubMed Central): Sedimentary biomarkers of human presence and taro cultivation reveal early horticulture in Remote Oceania

title: Seal-Hunters' Villages of the Tarkine
place: West Point (Nongor), Tarkine coast, northwest Tasmania, Australia
text: About 1,900 years ago, Aboriginal people on Tasmania's northwest coast began a more settled way of life that lasted until the 1830s. In summer, groups gathered in villages of huts beside rich spots such as West Point, next to an elephant seal colony, then split up in leaner winters. Their shell middens hold seal and shellfish remains but strikingly few fish bones.

source.name: Australian Government, Australian Heritage Database: Western Tasmania Aboriginal Cultural Landscape

dateLabel: About 1260 BCE (earliest dates for the site)
title: The Beach That Named Lapita
place: Site 13A, Foué peninsula, Koné, North Province, New Caledonia
text: The famous Lapita culture takes its name from a misspelled Kanak name for a beach in Koné. People began living on this narrow spit of land around 1260 BCE, leaving pottery, adzes and shell armbands. In 1952 excavators found finely decorated pots here and used radiocarbon dating to prove the site was far older than expected, with pottery resembling finds from Fiji, Tonga and Watom.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Lapita (13A)

title: Remote Oceania's Earliest Village?
place: Nanggu (SE-SZ-8), Nendö, Santa Cruz Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
text: On Nendö in the Santa Cruz Islands, a Lapita village beside Tepiai Lagoon was settled roughly 3,400 to 3,100 years ago and lived in for about a century. Excavated in 1971 by Roger Green, it is described as the earliest settlement yet found in Remote Oceania. Its pottery, stone adzes, gravers and animal bones offer clues about the very first colonists.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Nanggu (SE-SZ-8)

dateLabel: About 1340 BCE (oldest dates about 3,300 years ago)
title: Early Lapita Life on Babase
place: Kamgot, Babase Island, Anir Group, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
text: Kamgot, on a raised limestone shelf of Babase Island, stretches over 400 metres and is one of the few sites from the very start of Lapita, the oldest of four Lapita sites in the Anir group. Its oldest radiocarbon dates centre around 3,300 years ago. Diggers found decorated pottery, obsidian, shell fishhooks, rings and beads, engraved bone and drilled dog teeth.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Kamgot (ERA)

dateLabel: By about 650 BCE (no later than 2,600 years ago)
title: A Painted Pot From Vao
place: Vao Island, off Malakula, Malampa Province, Vanuatu
text: On little Vao Island, off Malakula, archaeologists found Late Lapita burials dated to no later than 2,600 years ago. They also pieced together a pot from 20 sherds. Its makers stamped toothed patterns on the upper half, then covered them with white paint and added red, partly hiding the stamped designs. The site was found in 2002 during heritage training with the Vanuatu Cultural Centre.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Vao

title: Mountains of Shells at Weipa
place: Wathayn, Albatross Bay, Weipa, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia
text: Around Albatross Bay on Cape York, Aboriginal people heaped up more than 500 shell mounds, the biggest over 10 metres high with up to 10,000 tonnes of shell. Radiocarbon dates from 70 mounds at Wathayn show mounds growing 2,300 to 1,800 years ago, a time once thought quiet. Aboriginal people today say the mounds were where shellfish were opened before the meat was carried away.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2017, via PubMed Central): Temporal variability in shell mound formation at Albatross Bay, northern Australia

dateLabel: About AD 87 (oldest pottery date, 1,863 years BP)
title: Pohnpei's Drowned First Villages?
text: Pottery, a sure sign of settlers, first appears on Pohnpei about 1,863 years before 1950, and on Kosrae a little earlier. But mangrove mud shows the sea around both islands has risen about 4.3 metres over 5,700 years as the land sank. Much early evidence already comes from tidal or underwater sites, so even older villages may lie below the waves.

source.name: PNAS (2022, via PubMed Central): Implications of anomalous relative sea-level rise for the peopling of Remote Oceania

title: Palau's Long Family Line
place: Ucheliungs burial cave, Rock Islands, Koror, Palau
text: People first lived on Palau's Rock Islands and Babeldaob about 3,200 years ago. DNA from a person buried in the Ucheliungs cave about 2,800 years ago shows roughly 60 percent East Asian and 40 percent Papuan ancestry, much like Palauans today. The two groups had mixed before reaching Palau, giving the islands the longest population continuity known in Remote Oceania.

source.name: Cell (2026, via PubMed Central): Papuan admixture predated the settlement of Palau

title: Schoolchildren Find a Lapita Village
place: Tamuarawai (EQS), Emirau Island, St Matthias Group, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
text: In 2006 a teacher, Mr K. Vito, and pupils from Rongol Top Up primary school on Emirau Island found old pottery. Photos sent to archaeologist G.R. Summerhayes showed it was Lapita, and digs followed. Dated to roughly 3,360 to 3,160 years ago, the village left shell fishhooks, net sinkers, octopus lures, beads and even a slingshot stone.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Tamuarawai (EQS)

title: Lapita Settlers Reach Maré
place: Kurin (LPO023), Maré, Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia
text: On a dune beside the reef on Maré, in the Loyalty Islands, Lapita people lived from about 1050–1000 BCE to 850–800 BCE. Their oldest dates come from a stone cooking oven. The site shows the Loyalty Islands were settled at roughly the same time as New Caledonia's main island. It was found in 1997 by Christophe Sand and F. Wadra of the Yéwéné Cultural Centre.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Kurin (LPO023)

dateLabel: About 910 BCE (cumulative date for first occupation)
title: New Pots on the Isle of Pines
place: St Maurice-Vatcha (KVO003), Vao, Isle of Pines, New Caledonia
text: On a dune at the southern tip of the Isle of Pines, Lapita settlers arrived around 910 BCE, just decades after others reached New Caledonia's main island. They left pottery, shell rings, beads and adzes. In the upper layers, incised pots seen as forerunners of the later Puen style appear beside Lapita ware, showing the old tradition flowing into a new one.

source.name: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Lapita Pottery Online Database: Vatcha (KVO003)

title: The Man Under the Bus Stop
place: Narrabeen, northern beaches, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: Digging beneath a bus shelter at Narrabeen revealed an Aboriginal man killed on the dunes about 4,000 years ago. Small stone points called backed microliths, plus injuries to his bones, showed he died from stone-tipped spears: the first archaeological evidence of death by spearing in Australia. It also revealed how these points were used, and hints at a ritual punishment.

source.name: Antiquity 81 (McDonald et al. 2007), Australian National University research portal: The first archaeological evidence for death by spearing in Australia

source2.name: Cambridge Core, Antiquity: The first archaeological evidence for death by spearing in Australia

title: A Turtle Made of Beeswax
place: Gunbilngmurrung, western Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Some rock art in Arnhem Land was made from beeswax rather than paint. A naturalistic beeswax turtle at Gunbilngmurrung, radiocarbon-dated in 1995 and confirmed by a second test in 2002, is more than 4,000 years old: the oldest visible image of confirmed age in Arnhem Land. Drawn in the early X-ray style, it even shows a thin-line backbone.

source.name: ANU Press, The Archaeology of Rock Art in Western Arnhem Land, Australia (2017), chapter 1

title: A New Toolkit at Murujuga
place: Dampier Archipelago (Murujuga), Pilbara, Western Australia, Australia
text: Before about 3,500 years ago, campsites in the Dampier Archipelago held scrapers, horsehoof cores and retouched flakes. After that, Aboriginal toolmakers added microliths, tula adzes and slugs. These smaller tools were probably fixed to handles rather than held in the hand, and many were made from stone brought in from outside the islands. Rock engravings here show spears, boomerangs and nets.

source.name: Australian Government, Australian Heritage Database: Dampier Archipelago (including Burrup Peninsula)

title: A Dingo Buried With Care
place: Curracurrang Rockshelter, Royal National Park, New South Wales, Australia
text: In a rockshelter about 30 km south of Sydney, a nearly complete dingo skeleton was buried about 2,000 years ago. Its teeth are unusually worn, hinting it ate harder food than wild dingoes. Researchers note that Aboriginal people usually buried dingoes much as they buried community members, sometimes beside people, and that some tame dingoes lived in camps.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2023, via PubMed Central): Dingoes, companions in life and death: The significance of archaeological canid burial practices in Australia

dateLabel: By about AD 250–400 (1,700–1,550 years BP at the latest)
title: Settling Lonely Pingelap Atoll
place: Pingelap Atoll, Pohnpei State, Federated States of Micronesia
text: Pingelap is an atoll of only 1.8 square kilometres, nearly 70 km from the nearest island. Radiocarbon dates show people were living there by 1,700–1,550 years ago at the latest, only a few centuries after Kosrae and Pohnpei were settled. Early layers hold shell tools, ornaments, heaps of sea-creature remains and burnt remains of crop plants.

source.name: Radiocarbon 61(3), Cambridge Core (Levin, Seikel and Miles 2019): A Partial Chronological Sequence of Human Habitation for Pingelap Atoll
